questions.question_text: The term that refers to the neglect of all alternate forms of pleasure apart from alcohol is
questions.explanation: Salience refers to the neglect of all leisure and other alternate form of pleasures apart from alcohol. One's life revolves around getting alcohol, storing it, saving money to buy it, making opportunities to drink etc. Narrowing of repertoire: A social drinker may drink in various situations at various places and may have various drinks of his choice. A dependent drinker will settle into a fixed setting, sticking to one beverage. This may help him maintain steady level of alcohol in blood without much fluctuation. Note that some widening of repertoire is inevitable in the career of an alcohol drinker - moving from weekends only to all days of the week etc.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of type 1 alcoholism, according to Cloninger?
questions.explanation: Type 1 alcoholism is milieu-limited (i.e., caused by environmental influences e.g. living with alcoholics). Thus it can be seen equally in both males and females. Subjects often experience a sense of loss of control, typical of alcoholism. They lack a strong family history of alcoholism and do not have high rates of criminality; the habitual use generally starts after 25 years of age.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?

options.text: Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium.
The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.
These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time.
The hallucinations usually last less than a week.
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign, and threatening.

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

correct_answers.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

questions.explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis: The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign, and threatening. The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the untrue nature. These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time. Delusions are usually secondary interpretations of the hallucinations. The patient is usually distressed, anxious, and restless. Unlike DTs those with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium. As an empirical timescale, hallucinations lasting for more than 6 months should initiate suspicion of other psychoses including schizophrenia. The hallucinations respond well and rapidly to antipsychotics. The prognosis is good provided that the person remains abstinent. But the evidence base for treating alcoholic hallucinosis is very poor.

questions.question_text: Which drug should be given as prophylaxis against irreversible neurological damage in all patients undergoing in-patient alcohol detoxification?
questions.explanation: It is generally advised that all patients undergoing in-patient detoxification should be given parenteral thiamine as prophylaxis for Wernicke's encephalopathy, which can be associated with irreversible amnesic syndrome in some individuals. This is given for 5 days and may be followed by oral vitamin B compound. The only Parenteral high potency B-complex vitamin therapy licensed in the UK is Pabrinex. Prophylactic treatments for patients at high risk of Wernicke's encephalopathy should be one pair IM/IV ampoules high potency B-Complex vitamins (Pabrinex) daily for 3-5 days.

questions.question_text: What is considered as a safe limit of weekly alcohol consumption in women?
questions.explanation: Safe limits for weekly consumption in males is up to 21 U a week; 21 to 49U is considered hazardous; more than 49U a week amounts to harmful use range. In females - up to 14U a week is safe; 14-35U being hazardous, and more than 35U being harmful.

questions.question_text: The amount of alcohol units in two pints (2 X 568ml) of beer that has a strength of 4% alcohol by volume (ABV) is
questions.explanation: A simple method is to multiply ABV in % (alcohol by volume) for a drink by the liters consumed. Thus two pints (2 X 568ml) of beer at 4% ABV contains 1.136 X 4 = 4.5U.

questions.question_text: The symptoms of alcohol withdrawal usually subside within
questions.explanation: In most alcohol dependent individuals the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal are mild to moderate and usually disappear within 5-7 days after the last drink.

questions.question_text: According to NICE guidelines, opioid detoxification with buprenorphine in an inpatient setting should last for
questions.explanation: The NICE guidelines indicate, that opioid detoxification in an inpatient setting may take place over a shorter time than in the community (suggesting 14-21 days for methadone and 7-14 days for buprenorphine) as the supporting element helps the patient to tolerate emerging withdrawal symptoms. As in the community, a stabilisation on the dose of a substitute opioid is first achieved, followed by gradual dose reduction; with additive medications judiciously prescribed for withdrawal symptoms if and as needed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is regarded as the most suitable screening tool for the hazardous use of alcohol in primary care settings?
questions.explanation: A recent systematic review 21 of the literature has concluded that the AUDIT is the best screening instrument for the whole range of alcohol problems in primary care.

questions.question_text: For detecting hazardous and dependent drinking in primary care, which one of the following is recommended as the best tool to use?
questions.explanation: AUDIT (Alcohol use disorders identification test) is designed to be used as a brief structured interview or self report questionnaire, which is suitable for general practice use. It has a sensitivity of about 83% among males and 65% among females in primary care settings.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old patient who has been dependent on alcohol meets with a road traffic accident and is admitted at an orthopaedic ward for a fractured wrist. Which of the following is correct with respect to his clinical state?

options.text: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually starts within 48 hours
The chances of having a delirium is highest after 5 days
Risk of seizure is maximal from day 3 to day 5.
Having withdrawal symptoms 5 days after abstinence is unusual
He will not have a seizure unless he has a head injury

correct_answer.text: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually starts within 48 hours

correct_answers.text: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually starts within 48 hours

questions.explanation: Withdrawal seizures (rum fits) occur within 6-48 hours of alcohol cessation; they are major motor seizures that take place during withdrawal in patients who normally have no seizures and have normal electroencephalograms (EEGs). These seizures are typically generalized and brief.

questions.question_text: Disulfiram inhibits which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, thus leading to acetaldehyde accumulation after drinking alcohol, which can cause extremely unpleasant side effects, leading to signs and symptoms such as flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations if alcohol is consumed. Continued drinking can lead to arrhythmias, hypertension and collapse. Therefore, the treating clinician must ensure that no alcohol has been consumed by patient 24 hours before commencing on treatment.

questions.question_text: Which class of drugs is recognised as the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are recognised as the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal. They are cross tolerant with alcohol and have anticonvulsant properties. They are typically given for seven days. Benzodiazepines are better than placebo for alcohol withdrawal for various outcomes including reducing the severity of withdrawal, reduction in the incidence of complications (delirium and seizures), completion of regimen and subsequent rehabilitation. The choice of which benzodiazepine to use depends on the circumstances of treatment; almost all benzodiazepines are shown to be efficacious in alcohol detoxification.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not associated with alcoholism?
questions.explanation: Binswanger's disease is a vascular dementia not directly linked to alcohol use.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the drug of choice in patients with an uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal syndrome?
questions.explanation: Chlordiazepoxide is the drug of choice in patients with uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal as it has a low dependence forming potential. A typical fixed regimen for covering uncomplicated withdrawal is 20 mgs q.d.s. of Chlordiazepoxide, reducing over approximately seven days. Additional titration using prn medication can be used in the first two days.

questions.question_text: You are called to A&E to see a man withdrawing from amphetamines. He is least likely to have
questions.explanation: Amphetamine withdrawal effects include dysphoric mood (crash) sometimes with suicidal ideation, fatigue, vivid, unpleasant dreams, increased appetite and hypersomnia besides psychomotor retardation/agitation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs often require direct supervision by the treating clinician when the treatment is commenced?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram acts as a deterrent. Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in the accumulation of acetaldehyde leading to signs and symptoms such as flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations if alcohol is consumed. This reaction is dose-dependent and if a large amount of alcohol is consumed, a more severe reaction may ensue leading to hypertension, collapse and even death. Therefore, the prescribing clinician must ensure that no alcohol has been consumed by patient 24 hours before commencing on treatment. Witnessing, or supervising, the taking of disulfiram is important for its efficacy. There is little evidence to guide how long patients should receive disulfiram but, generally, 3-6 months is advocated, or for as long any benefits are maintained.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature seen in hepatocerebral degeneration due to alcoholism?
questions.explanation: Dystonia is not a feature of hepatocerebral degeneration due to alcoholism. Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver failure is characterized by altered sensorium, frontal release signs, 'metabolic' flapping tremor, hyper-reflexia and extensor plantar responses. High mortality rates are noted; in those who make a partial recovery, a discrete neurological deficit characterised by tremor, choreoathetosis, dysarthria, gait ataxia, and dementia results. This is called as hepatocerebral degeneration. Enlargement and proliferation of protoplasmic astrocytes in the basal ganglia, thalamus, red nucleus, pons, and cerebellum, in the absence of neuronal loss or other glial changes, is noted.

questions.question_text: Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories through its actions at which of the following brain regions?
questions.explanation: Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories at hippocampus.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a marker for excess alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation: Increased MCV is a marker for excess alcohol use, with a sensitivity of 20- 50%, and specificity of 55-100%. It remains raised for 3-6 months, due to the 120-days lifespan of RBCs. It can turn false positive in patients with B12 or folate deficiency. GGT, a liver enzyme, has a sensitivity of 20- 90%, and specificity of 55- 100% to detect harmful use of alcohol. It remains raised for 2- 4 weeks. Other liver function tests are less specific for alcoholic-related liver damage. Elevated GGT can be a false positive finding in patients with other liver diseases and may remain raised in chronic alcoholic liver disease despite abstinence. CDT (Carbohydrate deficient transferase) has a sensitivity of 70%, and specificity of 95%. Increased levels of CDT occur in response to heavy drinking. A CDT test is more expensive than GGT test, and not available in some hospitals.

questions.question_text: Which of the following alcohol-related neurological damage has a specific association with red wine?
questions.explanation: Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome: It was first described by Carducci in 1898 in Italian red wine drinkers and by Marchiafava and Bignami in 1903. It occurs predominantly in malnourished alcoholics and is reported more often in male than female drinkers. Demyelination of the corpus callosum and adjacent subcortical white matter (Extrapontine myelinolysis) occurs. Dementia, spasticity, dysarthria, gait changes occur. Patients may lapse into coma and die, survive for many years with a dementia.

questions.question_text: If considering opioid detoxification, women who are pregnant or planning for pregnancy should consider treatment with which one of the following agents?
questions.explanation: Women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy should consider treatment with Methadone. Ideally, the mother should be encouraged to become abstinent prior to delivery--often this may not be possible. If pregnancy begins while a woman is taking high doses of methadone, the dosage should be reduced slowly (e.g., 1 mg every 3 days), and foetal monitoring must be carried out closely.

questions.question_text: Mr. X is a 45-year-old gentleman admitted to hospital with features of severe alcohol withdrawal, and laboratory investigations are arranged. Which one of the following finding is least likely to be found in his blood test results?
questions.explanation: When alcohol withdrawal is severe/complicated, it is important to arrange laboratory investigations in order to check for Macrocytosis, Low haemoglobin, Raised liver function tests, Leucocytosis and Thrombocytopenia. It is also important to check for dehydration, hyponatraemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesaemia, also hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia.

questions.question_text: Mr. X is a 45-year-old gentleman being treated with methadone for opioid dependence and recently took an overdose of methadone. Which drug should be administered in the event of methadone overdose?
questions.explanation: In the event of methadone overdose, Naloxone should be administered following BNF Guidelines. It may be given by intravenous, intramuscular or subcutaneous routes. The emergency services should always be called. 0.4-2 mg repeated at intervals of 2-3 minutes to a maximum of 10 mg should be tried. Naloxone is short acting, and the effect may reverse within 20 minutes to 1 hour, meaning that a patient can revert back into an overdose state. Therefore an ongoing medical monitoring should be provided after Naloxone administration.

questions.question_text: Mr. Smith was occasionally drinking at various places and was having various drinks of his choice until five years ago. But currently he would drink only at home sticking to vodka. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation: Narrowing of repertoire: A social drinker may drink in various situations at various places and may have various drinks of his choice. A dependent drinker will settle into a fixed setting, sticking to one beverage. This may help him maintain a steady level of alcohol in the blood without much fluctuation. Note that some widening of repertoire is inevitable in the career of an alcohol drinker - moving from weekends only to all days of the week etc.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman with significant alcohol-related problems does not recognise her responsibility or requirement to change her lifestyle. She even denies that her problems are alcohol related. She is in which of the following stages of change?
questions.explanation: During the precontemplation stage, patients do not even consider changing. Smokers who are in denial may not see that the advice applies to them personally. Patients with high cholesterol levels may feel 'immune' to the health problems that strike others. Obese patients may have tried unsuccessfully so many times to lose weight that they have simply given up.

questions.question_text: Which of the following feature is suggestive of schizophrenia instead of alcoholic hallucinosis in patients who have psychotic symptoms in a background of alcoholism?

options.text: Recurrence of hallucinations when drinking pattern is reinstated
Presence of thought disorder and affect incongruence.
Remission of psychotic episodes during abstinence
Onset of alcohol drinking clearly preceding the onset
Atypical or late age of onset of psychotic symptoms

correct_answer.text: Presence of thought disorder and affect incongruence.

correct_answers.text: Presence of thought disorder and affect incongruence.

questions.explanation: When considering alcoholic hallucinosis, differences from schizophrenia include atypical or late age of onset of psychotic symptoms, the onset of alcohol drinking clearly preceding the onset, remission of psychotic episodes during abstinence and lack of thought disorder and affect incongruence.

questions.question_text: Mr. X is a patient, who is alcohol abstinent for a long time but went back to the original pattern of heavy drinking in a surprisingly rapid manner after having a priming dose of alcohol. This state is described as;
questions.explanation: Reinstatement on relapse: This is a criterion stressed by Edward and Gross in their early description of alcohol dependence. A patient, who is abstinent for a long time, may go back to the original pattern of heavy drinking in a surprisingly rapid manner after having a priming dose of alcohol (relapse). Various explanations for this include: 1. abstinence violation effect - the cognition that 'I had a drink; so I am a drinker again' may force patients to reinstate full pattern of drinking 2. propensity to experience withdrawal symptoms may be carried over even through the period of abstinence in some individuals 3. Cues may trigger memory after priming dose, making compulsive drinking a behaviour.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of type II alcoholism, according to Cloninger?
questions.explanation: The features of type II alcoholism includes inheritance of the condition from the father, onset of alcohol-related problems before the age of 25 years, being found primarily in males, prominent history of criminality and poor prognosis characterized by an inability to achieve meaningful abstinence.

questions.question_text: Diminished or reverse tolerance is associated with all of the following except

options.text: When drinking alcohol after a period of abstinence
Metabolic problems such as liver disease

questions.explanation: Diminished tolerance is a notable phenomenon in drinkers. When drinking alcohol after a period of abstinence, the tolerance may revert to normal and might lead to quick intoxication. Older patients with brain damage may have curtailed neuroadaptation leading to reversed tolerance. Metabolic problems such as liver disease may apparently look like diminished tolerance.It may also be idiosyncratic in certain individuals.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs used to prevent relapse of alcohol use appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter system?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate is a synthetic taurine analogue, which appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter system. It is licensed to prevent relapse in alcohol use and has been found to have modest treatment effect.

questions.question_text: Sally is 10-weeks pregnant. She is on 70mg methadone daily and wants to stop taking it. What would you advise her to do?

options.text: Reduce and stop over next 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Women can present with opioid dependency at any stage in pregnancy. Stabilization on substitute methadone is the treatment of choice in any stage, as it has an established record of safe use in pregnancy. Opioid misuse in pregnancy can cause miscarriage and substitute prescribing carries a lower risk than continuing opioid misuse. Tapering of methadone is not recommend while someone is pregnant, as it can add to the chance of relapsing, developing withdrawals, and may precipitate miscarriage. Buprenorphine may be used in pregnancy, although there is less evidence for this and experts do not at present recommend routinely changing over mid pregnancy to this agent.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y was admitted to the orthopaedic ward three days ago after sustaining a fracture to his right femur following a road traffic accident. He became confused, distracted and agitated in 2-3 days following surgery. Routine blood and urine tests do not indicate infection or blood loss. The most likely diagnosis is;
questions.explanation: Delirium tremens is a toxic confusional state that occurs when alcohol withdrawal symptoms are severe. The symptoms typically peak between 72-96 hours after the last drink. The classical symptoms include confusion, distraction & clouding of consciousness, vivid hallucinations affecting every sensory modality and marked tremors. Clinical features also include fleeting paranoid delusions, agitation, sleep disturbances, signs of autonomic hyperactivity such as fever, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension.

questions.question_text: Following sudden cessation of alcohol on a dependent patient, the risk of seizure is high during which of the following time periods?
questions.explanation: As part of alcohol withdrawal symptoms, generalized seizures rarely occur , usually within 24 hours of cessation from alcohol. Benzodiazepines especially long-acting ones such as diazepam reduce the risk of seizures.

questions.question_text: A man who repeatedly presents to A& E with his girlfriend who is pregnant and heavy abuser of heroin. She plans to breast-feed following childbirth. Which medication is preferable to continue if she starts breast feeding?
questions.explanation: Methadone is considered compatible with breast-feeding. The Clinical Guidelines recommend that breast feeding should still be encouraged, but that with regards to methadone and breast feeding 'the dose is kept as low as possible while maintaining stability, and the infant monitored to avoid sedation.

questions.question_text: A man after completing his opioid detoxification is highly motivated to remain on treatment and wants advice about maintaining it. Which of the following drugs is best suited in this situation?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is recommended as a treatment option in detoxified, formerly opioid dependent subjects who are highly motivated to remain in an abstinence programme. For this group naltrexone treatment has been found by NICE to be a cost effective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse.

questions.question_text: Tim is taking heroin regularly. He has been tried unsuccessfully on methadone and buprenorphine. Choose the next best option.
questions.explanation: Current consensus guidelines suggest that patient should have 'specifically optimised higher dose oral methadone or buprenorphine maintenance treatment' after oral maintenance therapy before moving on to injectables. Injectable heroin and methadone treatments should be considered only for the minority of patients who are genuinely unresponsive to an optimised oral maintenance treatment approach. Injectable and oral substitute prescribing must be supported by locally commissioned and provided mechanisms for supervised consumption. Injectable drugs may present more risk of overdose than oral preparations and have a greater value on illicit markets and hence may require greater levels of supervision.

questions.question_text: Tom is on methadone treatment for heroin addiction. He attends A&E on two occasions as he is 'running out of supply of methadone' and demands treatment. What is the best course of action?
questions.explanation: It is possible that he is experiencing withdrawal symptoms, due to inadequate dose of methadone and possibly self medicating himself. The best course of action is to stabilise this patient by optimizing the dose of methadone. It is inadvisable to issue additional replacement opiates from the A&E Department. Liaising and passing on this information to the local drug service is what is essential so that they can review their prescribing and possibly increase the daily dose with closer supervision.

questions.question_text: Sally is physically dependent on dihydrocodeine, which she is taking for back pain. She wants to stop this and go back to work. What is the best course of action?
questions.explanation: Withdraw codeine cautiously in first instance, in conjunction with other pain management approaches (eg pregabalin, SNRI, psychology, TENS) and if unsuccessful then consider changing to methadone to facilitate withdrawal.

questions.question_text: The risk of developing alcohol problems for those with a positive family history compared to those without a family history of alcohol problems is increased by
questions.explanation: The risk of alcoholism in relatives of alcoholic probands is nearly four times as high as that of the general population.

questions.question_text: A patient is keen to come off heroin use but is anxious about experiencing withdrawal symptoms. Which of the following is best suited to support detoxification in this patient?
questions.explanation: Methadone treatment is more successful if carried out slowly or with a linear dose reduction; methadone can suppress withdrawal for 24 - 36 hours so once daily dosing is sufficient. Methadone may be desired by patients who do not want any withdrawal discomfort and/or anxious of experiencing a difficult withdrawal.

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with schizophrenia smoke?
questions.explanation: A quantitative review of 42 studies from 20 countries reported a 62% pooled rate of smoking in patients with schizophrenia, which was significantly elevated relative to general population (weighted average odds ratio, OR = 5.9; males = 7.2; females = 3.3).

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man states that he is currently drinking two bottles of wine a day. He is unable to cut down due to symptoms of insomnia, agitation and tremors. He is also reported to suffer from low mood, anhedonia and fatiguability. What would be the most appropriate treatment option?
questions.explanation: Alcohol detoxification is the most appropriate option to be tried first. Many alcohol withdrawal episodes take place without any medical or pharmacological treatment. In alcohol detoxification, the intended goals can be symptom suppression, avoiding complications and completion of regimen with subsequent abstinence.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a mechanism of action of Acamprosate in treating alcohol dependence?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate restores the altered balance between inhibitory and excitatory system seen in alcohol dependence.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old gentleman, with a history of opioid dependence, would like to consider pharmacological maintenance treatment along with psychosocial interventions. The most appropriate medication would be;
questions.explanation: For all patients who are opioid dependent with an informed decision to become abstinent, services should readily offer detoxification. Offer buprenorphine or methadone as first line treatment, with due consideration to service user's preference.

questions.question_text: Which of the following screening tools have only four questions?
questions.explanation: CAGE has only 4 questions. AUDIT has 10 questions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following substance is likely to be an active ingredient in the Ethiopian plant Catha edulis, whose leaves on chewing provide amphetamine-like stimulation?
questions.explanation: The stimulant effect of the Khat plant was originally attributed to cathine, but this was disputed by reports showing the plant extracts from fresh leaves contained another substance more active than cathine - called cathinone.

questions.question_text: Mr. P has a long standing history of substance misuse and has developed an ischaemic cerebrovascular disorder. Which of the following substance is most likely to precipitate it?
questions.explanation: The major complications of chronic use are cerebrovascular, epileptic and cardiac. The most common cerebrovascular diseases associated with cocaine use are non-haemorrhagic cerebral infarctions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is least suggestive of an opioid withdrawal state?
questions.explanation: Opioid withdrawal syndrome begins 6 to 8 hours after the last dose, peaks in 2 days and reduces in a week usually. The features include dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea, pupillary dilation, piloerection, or sweating, diarrhea, yawning, fever and insomnia.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old gentleman with a harmful alcohol habit is ambivalent about making a change. He is in
questions.explanation: This patient is currently contemplating a change in behaviour. During the contemplation stage, patients are ambivalent about changing. Giving up an enjoyed behavior causes them to feel a sense of loss despite the perceived gain.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most common during cocaine withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Effects of cocaine are short-lived with a rapid cessation of physiological effects occurring due to a rapid metabolism; this can induce a pattern of repeated use. Dysphoria (crash), anhedonia, anxiety, irritability hypersomnolence, and sometimes agitation usually end within 18 hours though in heavy dependent users this can last up to a week, peaking in 3 days. The characteristic feature is intense cravings for cocaine with a striking lack of much physical withdrawal symptoms.

questions.question_text: In Korsakoff syndrome, the type of memory that is most affected is
questions.explanation: Korsakoff's is characterized by marked deficits in anterograde and to some extent retrograde episodic memory, apathy, an intact sensorium, and relative preservation of other intellectual abilities such as attention, procedural memory and working memory.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common criterion for both 'substance abuse' and 'substance dependence' categories in diagnostic classifications?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of substance abuse is based on the consequences in physical, psychological, social and occupational aspects of a person's life. To diagnose dependence other criteria must also be met in addition to the impairment criteria.

questions.question_text: The route of cocaine administration that can produce a 'high' that can last up to 15 to 30 minutes is
questions.explanation: The duration of cocaine's euphoric effects ('high') depends upon the route of administration. The faster the absorption, the more intense the 'high'. The faster the absorption, the shorter the duration of action. The euphoria resulting from snorting is relatively slow in onset, and may last 15 to 30 minutes while that from smoking or mainlining may last 5 to 10 minutes.

questions.question_text: A man who has been abusing multiple substances now complains of frequent urination and passing blood in the urine. The most likely offending drug is;
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a derivative of phencyclidine, a popular street drug that is known as 'PCP' or 'angel dust'. Ketamine is less potent, and shorter acting compared with phencyclidine and is used as a dissociative anaesthetic in humans. The effects of ketamine include profound changes in consciousness and psychotomimetic symptoms, such as out-of-body experiences. Negative effects include increased heart and respiratory rates, nausea and vomiting, convulsions, temporary paralysis and hallucinations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true for long-term cocaine users?

options.text: Incidence of bipolar disorder is the same as in opiate addicts
Lifetime prevalence of any psychiatric disorders is 80%
Prevalence of co-morbid psychiatric disorder is 25%
Cocaine induced panic attacks occur in 15%

correct_answer.text: Lifetime prevalence of any psychiatric disorders is 80%

correct_answers.text: Lifetime prevalence of any psychiatric disorders is 80%

questions.explanation: At least 60-80% of cocaine users admit to mental health problems at some point when surveyed. Among these 18-20% have psychotic experiences.

questions.question_text: Among the following list, the drug least likely to cause physical or psychological dependence is
questions.explanation: Both physical and psychological dependence on hallucinogens are rare and not seen in present day clinical practice. This may be due to lack of reliable euphoria from hallucinogen use. Cannabis, on the other hand, causes well established psychological dependence. Physical dependence is rare in average users.

questions.question_text: You want to treat a pregnant woman in the 2nd trimester for opioid detoxification. Which one of the following is the suitable medication?
questions.explanation: The ideal time for detoxification is second trimester. Methadone is safer than other drugs; it can be continued throughout pregnancy. Babies born to mothers on heroin alone were more likely to be premature and small for dates. These effects could be reduced when the mother is stable on methadone.

questions.question_text: You are asked to see a 24-year-old man in the A&E. He is attempting to withdraw from heroin. Which of the following signs suggests advanced opioid withdrawal state?
questions.explanation: Opioid withdrawal symptoms may include lacrimation, rhinorrhea, agitation, perspiration, piloerection, vomiting, shivering, yawning and dilated pupils. Muscle spasms and twitching are signs of advanced opioid withdrawal state.

questions.question_text: In patients using recreational drugs, which of the following feature is characteristic of phencyclidine intoxication?
questions.explanation: PCP intoxication could cause the following features: Clinically significant assaultative behaviour, impulsiveness, unpredictability, psychomotor agitation, impaired judgment that developed during, or shortly after, phencyclidine use. Within an hour (less when smoked, 'snorted,' or used intravenously), two (or more) of the following signs: (1) vertical or horizontal nystagmus (2) hypertension or tachycardia (3) numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain (4) ataxia (5) dysarthria (6) muscle rigidity (7) seizures or coma (8) hyperacusis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with respect to the use of LSD?

options.text: Onset of action is delayed for 2 hours in most subjects
It is available as a prescribed drug

questions.explanation: LSD is primarily used via oral administration, but can be inhaled, injected, and transdermally applied. Onset of effects is rapid following intravenous administration (10 minutes). Following oral ingestion, onset of the first effects are experienced in 20-30 minutes. Frequent, repeated doses of LSD are unusual and therefore tolerance is not commonly seen.

questions.question_text: Identify the correct statement regarding treatment with naltrexone?

options.text: It has a much shorter half life than Naloxone
Combining naltrexone with psychological interventions provides limited additional benefit over naltrexone alone
Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal
Its effectiveness as a treatment for relapse prevention in opioid misusers is confirmed
Fatal overdose in those who relapse is rare

correct_answer.text: Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal

correct_answers.text: Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal

questions.explanation: Naltrexone might precipitate serious withdrawal syndrome if prescribed in an ongoing heroin user and therefore patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal, prior to giving the drug. Close monitoring is particularly important when naltrexone treatment is initiated because of the higher risk of a fatal overdose at this time.

questions.question_text: In phencyclidine intoxication, which of the following is least likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: PCP intoxication could cause the following features: Clinically significant assaultative behaviour, impulsiveness, unpredictability, psychomotor agitation, impaired judgment that developed during, or shortly after, phencyclidine use.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of opioid withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal syndrome include yawning, sweating, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, dilated pupils, piloerection, chills, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea/vomiting, crampy abdominal pains, diarrhoea, and muscle aches and pains.

questions.question_text: Which of the following could be used as a replacement therapy for a heroin user?
questions.explanation: Suboxone contains buprenorphine as well as the opioid antagonist naloxone to deter the abuse of tablets by intravenous injection.

questions.question_text: A 36-year-old cocaine user notices that the longer he uses the drug, the more of it is needed to achieve the same effect. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Tolerance refers to the pharmacological adaptation because of which a larger dose of a drug becomes necessary over time to achieve the same effect.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y is a regular drug user who presented to the A&E experiencing vivid, unpleasant dreams. He is most likely to be experiencing withdrawal from which of the following substances?
questions.explanation: The withdrawal effects of amphetamine include dysphoric mood (crash) sometimes with suicidal ideation, fatigue, vivid, unpleasant dreams, hypersomnia, increased appetite, psychomotor retardation and smaller pupils.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old lady with long standing history of alcoholism presents with ataxia, nystagmus and confusion. She was admitted to the medical ward. Which one among the following drugs should be used as prophylaxis in the further management of this case?
questions.explanation: This case has developed Wernicke's Encephalopathy due to alcohol misuse. It is advised that all patients undergoing in-patient detoxification should be given parenteral thiamine (Vitamin B1) as prophylaxis for Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about the pharmacokinetics of alcohol?

options.text: Drinks with more than 30% alcohol content are absorbed more readily than those with less concentration
Most alcohol is excreted unchanged in urine
Reduced gastric motility increases alcohol absorption
Females have less risk of intoxication for the same units consumed when compared to males
Pyloric stenosis decreases the absorption of alcohol

correct_answer.text: Pyloric stenosis decreases the absorption of alcohol

correct_answers.text: Pyloric stenosis decreases the absorption of alcohol

questions.explanation: The longer alcohol is exposed to gastric alcohol dehydrogenase greater will be its breakdown (and consequently less the blood levels). As a result, the presence of pyloric stenosis may reduce the chances of a rapid overshoot of alcohol in blood and intoxication.

questions.question_text: Which of the following signs is highlighted in the ICD-10 for a diagnosis of acute hallucinogen intoxication?
questions.explanation: Tachycardia, mydriasis, sweating, palpitations are some of the signs listed in ICD-10 for diagnosing acute hallucinogen intoxication.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum amount of alcohol per week that is advisable for a woman who is pregnant?
questions.explanation: Despite conceding that there is no evidence to support a specific limit, NICE recommends that women who are pregnant must drink no alcohol.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?

options.text: The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the untrue nature.
Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium.
These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time
The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign, and threatening.

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

correct_answers.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

questions.explanation: In alcoholic hallucinosis (AH), the hallucinations respond well and rapidly to antipsychotics. The prognosis is good provided that the person remains abstinent.

questions.question_text: A drunken man believes that his wife is cheating on him despite the absence of any evidence supporting his claim. This is a recognised feature of
questions.explanation: A delusional belief that ones partner is being unfaithful. This can occur as a part of a wider psychotic illness or secondary to organic brain damage associated with alcohol dependence or as a monosymptomatic delusional disorder (Othello syndrome).
